We hosted a webinar with a Quantum industry expert with 15 years experience in leading Quantum companies and large tech, as a follow-up to our recently published Quantum Deep dive note. This note is an edited transcript with key takeaways.

A key framework to understand the quantum landscape is the distinction between manufactured qubits and natural qubits. Manufactured qubits, such as superconducting, silicon spin, and topological, are engineered systems that benefit from fast speeds. However, they tend to suffer from higher noise and shorter coherence times. In contrast, natural qubits, including trapped ions and neutral atoms, are inherently identical with long coherence and strong noise resistance, while the main drawback being speed.

Currently, there are three leading modalities: superconducting (manufactured), trapped ions (natural) and neutral atoms (natural). Superconducting leads in scale, speed, and industrial maturity, supported by significant investment from large tech. Meanwhile, trapped ions and neutral atoms are advancing rapidly due to their superior qubit quality and natural ability to perform long-range interactions. Other modalities, such as spin qubits and photonic, are still earlier in development but show scaling potential, while topological represent a high-risk, high-reward approach that remains far from practical implementation.

The trade-off between speed and accuracy influences application fit. Problems that require repeated sampling to estimate real-valued outputs, such as chemistry simulations, materials science, favor fast systems like superconducting. Problems requiring a discrete correct answer, such as cryptography or combinatorial optimization, favor the higher fidelity of natural qubits. While IBM expects Quantum Advantage will be achieved this year, large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing is still many many years away. Progress depends on key milestones incl. development of logical qubits, logical gates, and scalable error-corrected systems.

Quantum computing is highly capital intensive. As a result, the dominant model will likely be cloud-based, rather than widespread ownership of machines. Early demand is driven by academia, government, and research fields with growing interest from industries like finance, logistics, and optimization.

Competitive dynamics favor large technology companies such as IBM and Google due to their access to capital, infrastructure, and talent. IBM, in particular, has a strong advantage in software and ecosystem like Qiskit, though its hardware leadership is increasingly challenged by higher-quality natural qubit systems. Startups are more likely to succeed through specialization, partnerships, or government-backed initiatives rather than competing head-on at full scale.

Overall, the industry is likely to evolve into a multi-modality ecosystem, where both manufactured and natural qubit coexist, each optimized for different applications, with hybrid quantum-classical computing emerging as the most practical path forward.

MN: Good morning, everyone. I'm Mark Newman, Bernstein's US IT Hardware Analyst. And today, we have the pleasure of hosting this webinar with a Technology Manager in the Quantum Computing Industry, who has 15 years experience in leading Quantum companies and large tech. At both companies, he worked on Quantum, so he has a wealth of knowledge and experience in quantum. And he is not biased because he is working for a non-profit currently. Expert, thank you very much for joining us. Anything else you'd like to add in terms of your background?

Expert: Yeah, absolutely. I've worked in the quantum computing industry and academia for the last 15 years or so. My career is sort of taking me up the whole stack that makes a viable quantum computer. I started off much more focused on hardware, even though I am a theoretical physicist by training, and then slowly over time moved to more system-level considerations, and then nowadays I work more on the software applications and algorithm side. My primary research expertise and focus for the last decade has been on characterization and benchmarking of quantum computers, so really understanding not only what they are capable of doing now, but what we can learn now to tell us about what they might be capable of in the near-term future and in the far-term future. So that's really been my focus.

MN: Great, thanks very much, Expert. And a reminder for everyone joining on the call, we do have a pigeonhole link where you can enter your own questions. I'm going to start off with a bunch of my own questions, and I'll refer to that later in the call to get some investor questions in as well. So let's get started. I'd like to start off talking about all the different, approaches, or what's referred to as the modalities for quantum. So, you have a lot of experience here, in quantum. You're neutral, as you said, working at a non-profit currently. If you had to rank the six modalities, can we talk about each of the six modalities and talk about them in terms of which ones you think have the best chance of success going forwards? I'll just list them all — superconducting, trapped ion, neutral atom, silicon spin, photonics, and topological.

Expert: Yeah, absolutely. So, I think, before I go into that, I want to put in a few caveat statements. Quantum computing as an industry is not necessarily following the path that classical computing and traditional computing has, in the sense that when you look at the early, early, early days of classical computing, when we had vacuum tubes and these sort of massive-scale systems, the industry was really revolutionized by the transistor. And it sort of unified around this single architecture that was going to be the one moving forward. That could happen in quantum computing, absolutely, and I think some of the modalities you mentioned there, even some that aren't on that list, that are even less solidified now, could have that kind of impact. But at the moment, we don't anticipate that necessarily in the next 10 or 15 years. It's one of these situations where an absolute revolution in science and in physics could cause this amalgamation or homogenization of the architecture. But right now, in my view, there's no clear winner in terms of the long-term bet. I think each architecture has their advantages and disadvantages, and it's a hard engineering and a hard science problem to overcome the roadblocks that they each have to getting to a large-scale quantum computer. There certainly are ones that are leading right now and ahead of the game. But these sort of revolutions do even happen on a small scale. Like, I'm gonna place neutral atoms somewhere, and if we had this call two years ago, they would have been in a completely different location on the scale. So, these kind of things can happen, just keep that in mind, that information needs to be refreshed periodically.

Expert: I like to break things into two buckets, into manufactured qubits and natural qubits. So manufactured qubits are superconducting qubits, the spin qubits, and the topological. The natural qubits are the trapped ions and neutral atoms. And then, kind of in the middle is photonic. Photonic qubits are “natural,” because they're light. But they require manufactured waveguides, manufactured substrates to live in. Now, this is actually also true of trapped ions, trapped neutral atoms, they have manufactured traps that they live in. So, the lines are all a little bit blurry here, right? But the reason this distinction is important is because it really impacts the quality of the individual qubits themselves.

With the natural ones, where you would see the trapped ions, the neutral atoms, and the photonic qubits, these qubits themselves have really good properties. One, they're consistent, every single one of them is the same in the world. And that makes a big difference about designing your control architecture, so the higher level stuff in the stack that controls the quantum is much more reliable, right? If you put 50 atoms in a trap, you know that all 50 are more or less the same to levels of accuracy that you don't really care about. Because they're natural the parts of their system that we use to store information also have

very natural properties. They're naturally long-lived, so they have good coherence times, which means that we can store the information for a long time. They're naturally robust to error, because again, these are systems that exist in the isolated world, independent of us creating them. So they have a lot of nice properties like that. The flip side is that all those properties that make them nice make them very hard to control. The control is very slow, so you think about the operation rate of these natural qubits, the ions and the atoms, it's at the... you can repeat a computation at most at a 1Hz repetition rate, so once per second. Some of this is engineering challenges, and these groups are working very hard to overcome them, right? But a lot of it is just the physical, natural operational speed of these devices is much slower. I'll touch on that in a bit.

Expert: By contrast, the manufactured qubits, they have much faster operation rates, because we are making that to be the case, right? So they operate at kilohertz, or even megahertz repetition rates, where we can repeat computations at a much faster timescale. The natural clock speed of the operations are also much faster, because again, we've designed the system to be the way we want. Where they fail, so where the superconductors, the spin qubits, and the Majoranas suffer, is that they, don't have as nice natural properties, with the exception of the Majoranas, which I'll get to in a second. But the superconducting and spin qubits are naturally noisier, they're not as consistent. When you make two superconducting qubits, for instance, even if you try to make them the same, you're not going to. There's a roughly 10% spread in fabrication, typically. That means your control systems have to be a lot more robust and work in a much larger bandwidth because they have to adapt naturally to the spread and the qubit properties. They don't have as good coherence times either. Because they're these macroscopic manufactured systems, they're much more susceptible to noise in the environment, and they have to be much more carefully isolated. And all of this means that typically the manufactured qubits are going to have worse properties. They're going to have worse error rates, as we call them, per operation. They're going to have worse coherence times, and the benefit for them is really the speed versus quality of the natural qubits.

Now, if we go on to dive into the details, each one in particular, the way I view it right now is sort of a three-way tie at the top, and it's hard to really say which one is leading, because it really depends on what you're looking for. And that three-way tie is between superconducting qubits, trapped ions, and neutral atoms. Two years ago, I would have put neutral atoms probably at the bottom of the whole list, right? In the last 3 years, there's been really revolutionary work out of the Harvard and MIT collaboration that has a spin-out company, QuEra, and they've really pushed the field. But it's important to caveat that they're so far the only ones who can get this good performance out of neutral atoms, whereas we see multiple trapped ion groups and multiple superconducting groups in industry and academia demonstrating good performance overall.

The superconductors win on speed, in the sense that if you want to do many, many repetitions of a circuit of a computation, which is something you naturally need to do for quantum computing - you can do that orders of magnitude, factors of a thousand, faster than anywhere else on them. They also have one of the largest scale computers, hundreds of qubits, and their quality has improved drastically in the last 5 years. So the quality of the gates is good, the reproducibility and robustness of the gates is very good. They're certainly, very ahead right now overall. So they're just maybe the 1A, right? The problem with them is the long-term vision is a little bit more murky. Because they're manufactured planar devices that exist on a flat plane, it's very hard to engineer interactions that aren't nearest neighbor, aren't between two qubits that are next to each other. And what we believe is that these longer-range interactions are necessary to do better error correction codes that will lower all the error rates to be where we can reach this fault-tolerant logical quantum computer that is going to be able to solve the applications we really care about. So there's tremendous savings in the number of physical qubits you need to make one logical qubit if you can enable these long-range interactions. That naturally just doesn't happen in superconducting qubits. Groups like the big industrial people like IBM and Google are working on finding ways to be able to do that. And I actually just saw this startup in Europe, IQM, has just released today their roadmap for that, for how they will enable these long-range interactions. So that's where I think things get a little murky. It's a lot of, to be frank, world-first demonstrations anywhere, even outside of academia, that has to be done for these groups to achieve that.

But, preliminary results that we have seen publicly look good, so they are on their pathway, but it is a big engineering and technical challenge. The ions and atoms naturally can do this, either by moving the ions around, or moving the atoms around as well, which are slightly different technologies to do that. So they can enable these long-range interactions, these multi-qubit connections, very naturally. And we'll see, probably in the next couple years, very quickly demonstrations from these groups, of those logical or early fault-tolerant demonstrations. But it's going to be hard for them to overcome this, the slowness of their sampling rates. So for applications like chemistry, material science that require estimation of a real number, where you need, you know, to some precision that's given by how many times you can repeat the computation. They're going to struggle, because the computations are going to take a thousand times longer. It's really a trade-off here, but there are applications that don't need that, like factoring, that just need the answer once, right? As long as you get it. So, you know, it really is application-dependent which one is going to be a long-term winner.

Expert: Spin qubits, photonics are at a much earlier stage, even though they've been explored for just as long, and photonic quantum computing was one of the first proposals. Photonic quantum computing has always, struggled with being able to interact photons. They naturally don't interact, so doing gates between the qubits is very hard, and that's still a problem. You have some companies that are exploring it, they have proposals, but we don't really see a lot of actual demonstrations coming out of those, so it's hard to judge where they're really at. Similarly, spin qubits are notoriously noisy and dirty and just difficult to manage. Once you can solve the problem of how do you make a high-quality spin qubit, how you can make interaction between two of them, it's very easy to scale because it's naturally semiconductor tech. We haven't gotten to that stage yet where we can actually leverage the scaling advantages from semiconductor tech. So I've put those at a joint, sort of, 4-5 area of that list. A lot of groups are looking at these now, especially in industry. You have Photonic Inc in Canada, you have Quandela in France, looking at this hybrid mode of both spin and photonics, using spins as the logical memory but doing all interactions via flying photonic qubits. No one has actually demonstrated that yet, so again, this is one of these long-term visions, but it's a way to kind of overcome the worst parts of both architectures and utilize the best parts of the two: use the naturally high coherence time of a spin, but its inability to interact with anything, then use the photons as information carriers to do that long-range interaction between spins. It's a long-term bet, we don't know if it'll pay off, but it's what some of the people are pivoting to.

Expert: And then the last, to be honest in my view right now, is the Majoranas. Not the last because of its promise. Topological qubits like Majoranas at Microsoft are doing work, I mean, they solve a lot of problems naturally, because they're naturally protected from noise and from error. But, they're very, very far away from being a real demonstration. No one's been able to demonstrate a single qubit, despite what you might see in popular press when you boil down to the technical demonstrations. We're at the stage of demonstrating the possibility of a classical logical information carrier, so a bit existing in the system. Topological physics is, of course, very hard to demonstrate. It requires these heterogeneous structures of superconductors and semiconductors that are notoriously difficult to manufacture, so there's a lot of outstanding problems. So I think they're one of those ones that are poised for revolution. If they can demonstrate this and it works, they will very quickly catch up with the rest of the field. But it is a big "if?", and it is, it would be a Nobel Prize-level kind of demonstration.

MN: Okay, great. So, in conclusion, top three being superconducting, trapped ion, and neutral atom, those are the top three. I wanted to just circle back on something you said that was interesting. You were saying that certain types of applications may be better served by superconducting because of speed, versus some which may be better served by something like trapped ion or neutral atom. Could you just double-click on that in terms of which type of application will be better for each type?
Expert: Absolutely, so I'll give a very technical description, but try to make it understandable, and then...
MN: Not too technical.

Expert: Not too technical. Yeah, so basically, well, I think it's interesting because it kind of ties into the way people think about modern AI and generative learning. If the application you need wants a real number, so like an energy from a chemical molecule, or a reaction rate from a surface material. Those are going to require a lot of shots because you're going to need to estimate that real number to an accuracy that is given by 1 over the number of repetitions, the number of shots. So that's where you need something that's fast. Those kinds of applications need many, many samples, and you can often get away with not being so accurate because there's techniques you can do to try to minimize the impact of your errors, the errors in your computation. You're competing against classical algorithms that are by their nature, also approximate. It's okay to not always be correct if you can get a lot of data.

Expert: On the flip side, applications that don't want real numbers but a distribution of outcomes, so that's things like factoring, where you're just looking for the factors, right? You're gonna get some distribution of numbers that could be the factor, or pairs of numbers, and you want the one that is the pair. And it's gonna have the highest probability, hopefully, that you get that right number. Or things like optimization problems, where you're looking for the optimal path for a salesman to take, even though that's too hard a problem, but things like that, where there's a discrete answer that comes out at the end that has a binary representation. Those are where you want high accuracy because you want the probability of getting the right answer to be really high. But you don't actually need to take a lot of shots, because once you get the right answer, you're done.
MN: What's an example of what you said for factoring? What's a real-life example there?

Expert: Factoring is useful for encryption breaking, so if you want to break RSA or elliptic curve cryptography, Shor's algorithm, which is the one of the first quantum algorithms developed, will break that by factoring the co-primes, products of two prime numbers, that go into the public key. For RSA, for instance, you want to make sure the algorithm, even the noisy version, has a high probability of giving you that right answer immediately. That's where you want the maximum quality you can get, because once you've run it once, gotten the answer, run it twice, however small number of times it takes, once you get the answer, you're done. You don't ever need to run it again. So that's where the quality over speed is important. So cracking codes, these types of things, trapped ion and neutral atom are better. But for chemistry, materials science, you need more shots and more speed, so superconducting is potentially better. It's not a hard and fast, right? There are ways to use the sampling version for material science, for discovery science, for chemistry, and there's machine learning applications, for instance, that don't need real numbers but quality samples? It's not hard and fast, but that's sort of, in my view, like a broad picture categorization.

You want high-quality samples, and then you can... and this is where I will lead into some combination of classical and quantum, where with those high-quality samples, you can feed those into classical algorithms that do the bulk of the optimization, and what the quantum is doing is preparing these high-quality initial sample states that they use. Expert: Absolutely, yeah, I think so.

MN: Okay, and which metric should we actually be looking at when we're comparing progress between companies here? Because there's a lot of numbers that are thrown out by some of these competitors, IBM, etc. So, is it physical qubit count? Is it two-qubit gate fidelity? Is it coherence time? You know, what are the ones that we should be looking at?

Expert: Yeah, so a physical qubit count isn't in and of itself really useful. I would say this is an evolving problem right now. Like, this is what my research is on, right? People are working on ways to better quantify things. A concept like what people would call an active volume, so it's how many qubits can be actively used at once in a computation, is more useful. For a manufactured qubit, it's very easy to build a thousand qubits, but you're not going to be able to control them all, or use them all. For instance, for IBM devices, you want to see that you can actually create a large quantum state across all the qubits, so you want to be able to run an algorithm that has all of them involved. I think physical qubit count is useful, obviously, because you need a big enough system to do operations, to do something useful or interesting, but it has to be actively available or useful. When it comes to gate fidelities, the field has kind of moved away from the single qubit gate fidelity, et cetera, being that useful a metric. What we really look at now is the two-qubit gate fidelity, not in isolation, but in the context of a larger operation. So, running a simultaneous operation on 15 qubits, on 20 qubits, on 100 qubits. And the reason for that is all of the architectures suffer from what people call crosstalk, which is when a gate over here unintentionally impacts a gate over there, unintentionally changing the way it performs. But in reality, no algorithm happens gate by gate by gate by gate by gate. You're gonna use as much of the real estate as you can simultaneously to minimize computation time, right? So that's where you want to look at metrics. I mean, I developed these ones at IBM, Layer Fidelity and others, but they're applied broadly, looking at simultaneous performance that plays into some of the other architectures as well.

Expert: The superconducting qubits can do a lot of gates at once, not all as high quality, a lot more impact of this crosstalk. Neutral atoms, trapped ions, can't do as many at the same time. What they do is they move ions around, so they have to do subsets of these operations, but they're all much higher quality. So these kind of metrics of, for example, how if you did all 10 gates at once what the performance would be; how they're moving the ions around, how they're moving the atoms around; how they're handling those transformations, scheduling the different operations sequentially. All those things impact performance of algorithms. These sort of system-scale metrics that can be boiled down to a single number are useful because they give you an overall idea of quality. But as a characterization person, I have to say, the unfortunate reality is all of these metrics are designed to be average, right? It's how good on average would you do? So your actual application will differ. And that's the hardest problem right now in characterization, it's figuring out a better way to connect to specific application performance.
MN: Great, thanks, and which modality would you say, is the most underappreciated right now? Which has most momentum, potentially one that the market is not taking enough notice of?

Expert: That's a good question. I would say the market's taken very well to most of them. I would say there's some more niche approaches to superconducting qubits that do what are called bosonic encodings, so rather than encode the information in a superconducting qubit, they encode it in a microwave resonator, so in light but at the microwave frequency, and they use the qubits for control. And you have companies like Alice & Bob in France, Nord Quantique in Canada, Quantum Circuits, who just got bought out by D-Wave in the US, they were doing this. And that has a lot of promise because it gives you high coherence time, and it gives you naturally error-robust properties. It's a bit hard to control. I think maybe those are still a little bit underappreciated for their potential in the near-ish term. They may not be the longest long-term bet, but on the middle ground scale, they might be able to demonstrate some useful devices quicker, even if then they run into scaling problems of their own.

MN: Okay, thanks very much. I'd like to move on to the next topic, which is around the timeline to quantum supremacy. Can you walk through a base case for timeline in terms of when we get to this kind of desirable quantum advantage on really meaningful, commercially relevant problems?

Expert: Yeah, I think there's two or maybe three gates. There's quantum advantage on anything that robustly stands the test of time over more than two months. There's quantum advantage on something commercially viable, and I would say that might be a business or research application. Large-scale quantum advantage is the third stage, where we're solving very hard problems routinely. Depending on who you ask, you're gonna get different answers. For instance, IBM claims that they'll get that first kind of quantum advantage, maybe even the second one, this year. On the flip side, the NIST estimates it's coming in or around 2035 in their recommendation for adopting post-quantum cryptography, cryptography that's resilient to quantum attacks. Essentially they're thinking that the possibility exists by 2035 that you could have a cryptographically relevant quantum computer that can run Shor's algorithm. That's a very, very large scale and complicated machine. I think all of this should be taken with a grain of salt. My view, we're probably looking at a 15-year time frame before we're at the scale where we're doing Shor's algorithm kind of problems. Maybe 20 years. Even here, I feel like I'm being a little bit optimistic. And there's really that question of what happens in the in-between. I personally find timelining very hard right now because we're at the cusp of a transition from purely physical devices, where we're operating just on the bare qubits, to these early fault-tolerant logical devices, where we're starting to encode qubits together to do redundant encoding to get higher quality logical, qubits. And I'm worried what we don't know right now is really the performance of those initial devices, because right now, first groups are starting to demonstrate it in the industry. If that works well, I think we can see that I would be comfortable saying is limited quantum advantage in some specific cases in the next 5 years, probably in research science but not so much in commercially applicable things like financial market prediction or fraud detection. One thing I do want to point out, though, is we always think about advantage as better, as faster, as cheaper, as less energy. But advantage can also mean different things, and what we're really starting to see that now is that quantum computers, even noisy ones, can unlock different ways of preprocessing information, which we can then hand off to a classical computer to do the actual processing. I feel like in the next 5 years, you're going to see that kind of advantage where the quantum computer is one part of an overall HPC system, even though it's not doing the heavy lifting. It's just doing one small part that gives a difference in the outcome. It might not be cheaper, it might not be faster, but it could be different in a way that is useful to the application. And I think in some of the things that do with outlier detection, like fraud detection, that could be useful because they potentially change the way we encode data, learn data, and separate classes of data. I think we're almost there, to be honest, but none of this touches on just the accessibility of all of this, and whether or not we're going to be able to use it realistically in a deployed environment. The existing cloud infrastructures are slow, so there are lots of other implementation questions that come into meeting real value. But in terms of the pen and paper, I can say that this is doing something different and slightly better, or meets my requirements better. I would say in the next 5 years, we should hopefully see that.
MN: And any more specifics in terms of concrete signposts that we can look for between now and this kind of more meaningful quantum supremacy?

Expert: I think a lot of those signposts are going to be very “technical” in nature because they're going to be about demonstration of error correction. I don't really take application demonstrations as necessarily the best signposts, because it's very hard to do cross-platform comparison, or cross-application comparison in quantum computing, because the primitives that underlie algorithms are very different. But if you're talking more broadly you've got to look at where the hardware is going. When companies announce, “Okay, we have a logical qubit, and it has this fidelity,” that's the first signpost. Great. They're halfway there. When they say, “Okay, we have a logical gate,” now that's a big step. “Now we can do two encoded, protected operations between two different logical qubits.” That's the next big step. And then you're looking for, “Okay, now we have tiled a system, we have 10 logical qubits, and we can do gates between all of them.” So those technology signposts are pointing along that long-term pathway. Because the tricky part with these long-term algorithms, like Shor’s algorithm, like some of the ones that do very high-performance chemistry and material science, is that there are no in-between. It's either all or nothing. What you're looking for is the building blocks of finally being able to do that algorithm coming into play.
